key_concept: A seed is non-albuminous (exalbuminous) when the developing embryo uses up the endosperm completely before the seed matures. A seed is albuminous when some endosperm remains in the mature seed.
steps: Recall the definitions. In albuminous seeds, part of the endosperm survives in the mature seed as stored food. In non-albuminous seeds, the embryo consumes all the endosperm during development.
In non-albuminous seeds, the food is stored mainly in the cotyledons instead, which is why such seeds have thick, fleshy cotyledons.
Wheat: a cereal grain with a large persistent endosperm, so it is albuminous.
Maize: also a cereal with a persistent starchy endosperm, so it is albuminous.
Barley: likewise a cereal with a persistent endosperm, so it is albuminous.
Pea: the endosperm is fully absorbed and food is stored in the two fleshy cotyledons, so it is non-albuminous.
Hence pea is the only plant in the list that produces non-albuminous seeds.
why_not_others: Wheat, maize and barley are all cereals (grasses), and cereal grains keep a large starchy endosperm at maturity, so all three have albuminous seeds.
common_trap: Students sometimes mix up the two terms and think 'non-albuminous' means the seed never formed an endosperm. In fact, the endosperm does form but is used up during seed development.
time_saving_tip: Three options are cereals, which are always albuminous, so the odd one out is the legume. Remember the examples: pea, groundnut and beans are non-albuminous, while wheat, maize, barley, castor and sunflower are albuminous.
